question: A 25-year-old man presents with a painful, oedematous glans penis that cannot be covered by the retracted foreskin, which has been in this position for four hours following catheterisation. What is the correct immediate management?

answers.text: Apply topical steroid cream and advise the patient to reduce it himself at home

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical steroids treat phimosis, not paraphimosis; home management is inappropriate — paraphimosis causes progressive venous and lymphatic obstruction that will worsen and may lead to glans ischaemia.

answers.text: Attempt immediate manual reduction under analgesia or anaesthesia; if unsuccessful, perform a dorsal slit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Paraphimosis is a urological emergency. Manual reduction (compressing the glans to reduce oedema and slipping the prepuce forward) under adequate analgesia is first-line; a dorsal slit is needed if this fails. Formal circumcision is deferred to a later date.

answers.text: Arrange elective outpatient circumcision within four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Elective circumcision is the definitive treatment after the acute episode, but immediate manual reduction is required now — a four-week wait risks glans necrosis.

answers.text: Apply a tight tourniquet to the base of the penis to reduce venous engorgement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A tourniquet would further compromise blood flow and cause irreversible ischaemia — it is absolutely contraindicated. Manual reduction is the correct approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: Paraphimosis — the foreskin trapped behind the glans — is a surgical emergency. Progressive oedema causes venous obstruction and glans ischaemia if not reduced immediately. Manual reduction is the priority.
Well done. Paraphimosis is an emergency: manual reduction first (compress the glans, slide the foreskin forward), dorsal slit if that fails. Elective circumcision can follow.
